Substitution into the inertial metric of [F1, F2], using $\cosh^2\theta-\sinh^2\theta=1$, cancels the mixed terms and yields the displayed pullback metric. For $d\rho=dy=dz=0$, the proper-time line element and adopted clock rule [F4] give $d\tau/dT=a\rho/c^2$.

Along a stationary worldline set $\eta=c\tau/\rho=aT/c$. Its inertial coordinates are $(\rho\sinh\eta,\rho\cosh\eta)$. For a radial null curve, set $dy=dz=0$ and $ds^2=0$ in the metric of step 2.1. Since $a,\rho,c$ are positive, this gives $d\rho/dT=\pm a\rho/c$. By [F10], $d(\log\rho)/dT=\pm a/c$; integration between its endpoint radii gives $\Delta T=(c/a)|\log(\rho_R/\rho_E)|$, finite for positive finite radii. Over a common nonzero Rindler-time interval $\Delta T$, step 2.1 gives $\Delta\tau_E=(a\rho_E/c^2)\Delta T$ and $\Delta\tau_R=(a\rho_R/c^2)\Delta T$. Their ratio is $\rho_R/\rho_E$. If the radii coincide the two increments agree; for distinct positive radii the ratio is positive and finite.

Under [A2] these contractions are the instantaneous received angular frequencies; their finite-apparatus interpretation retains the local ray-regime and short-observation qualifications of that postulate. Differentiating the shell identity with $\dot{\mathbf p}=F_0e_1$ gives $2\mathcal E\dot{\mathcal E}=2c^2p_1F_0$, hence $\dot{\mathcal E}=c^2p_1F_0/\mathcal E=F_0v_1$, as required by [F3]. Since $m,c>0$, the square-root denominator is at least $mc>0$, and [F5] gives subluminal motion.

Hence $\dot{\mathbf x}_\perp=c\mathbf p_\perp/\sqrt{\Pi^2+p_1^2}=\mathbf v_\perp$. At $t=0$ both position increments vanish, so these formulas have the prescribed initial position and velocity.

If $F_0=0$, [F3] makes $\mathbf p$ and $\mathcal E$ constant, so the displayed free position has derivative $c^2\mathbf p_0/\mathcal E(0)=\mathbf v$ and the initial position. Its speed is below $c$ by [F5].

The same component definition gives $\mathbf v_d\times\mathbf E= (E_0^2/B_0)e_3$, so the magnetic formula gives $\mathbf B'=\gamma_d(B_0-E_0^2/(B_0c^2))e_3=\mathbf B/\gamma_d$, using $1-|\mathbf v_d|^2/c^2=\gamma_d^{-2}$.

The primed field is uniform magnetic by step 2.1, so [F5] supplies its unique global orbit. The action in [A1] is unchanged by the boost: [F8] preserves the metric term, and pulling the one-form potential back by the coordinate change preserves its line integral. Thus stationary curves map to stationary curves, and under [A3], [F2] gives the covariant force equation in either chart. Applying the inverse Lorentz map therefore gives a laboratory worldline with the original initial data. Conversely, any laboratory solution transforms to a primed solution and coincides with the unique [F5] orbit; hence all laboratory solutions are exactly the inverse boosts of those magnetic orbits.

With $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf v_d/c$, the inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ from [F11] applied to the time-coordinate formula [F9] gives $t=\gamma_d(t'+\mathbf v_d\cdot\mathbf x'/c^2)$. Differentiating along the magnetic-frame orbit gives $dt/dt'=\gamma_d(1+\mathbf v_d\cdot\mathbf v'/c^2)$. Since its speed satisfies $|\mathbf v'|<c$ by [F5, F6], this derivative is at least $\gamma_d(1-|\mathbf v_d|/c)>0$. The positive lower bound makes $t$ strictly increasing and unbounded in both directions as $t'$ ranges over $\mathbb R$; thus the inverse-boosted curve is defined as a laboratory-time orbit for all real $t$.

Finally, $\mathbf v_d\times\mathbf B=-\mathbf E$ from step 2.1, so the laboratory force in [F3] under [A3] vanishes at constant $\mathbf v=\mathbf v_d$. The corresponding momentum is constant and its speed is subluminal by step 2.1. This exhibits one exact drift solution; step 3.1 shows that general initial data instead produce inverse-boosted magnetic orbits. No assertion is made about null or supercritical fields.
